title: Daily trend-flip rules on perps: is waiting for confirmation worth it, and what broke when you went live?
author: tommy_johnsen
selftext:
I'm building a small read-only research desk on my own server. Right now it only paper trades and sends me alerts, nothing live. Before I trust any of it I'd like to hear from people who've actually run this kind of thing.

Two questions:

1. If you trade daily trend-flip rules on crypto perps, how much of the move do you give up by waiting for a 3-candle confirmation? Did it still pay after fees, or did the lag eat most of the edge?
2. For anyone who went from paper trading to live auto-trading, what broke first? Slippage, fills, API quirks, or you overriding the system?

Real numbers or war stories are welcome. I'd rather learn from your mistakes than make them all myself.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: fills break first, nearly always. paper hands you the price you saw, live hands you what's left after everyone reacted to the same candle, and a trend flip fires exactly when they all do. that's why I made Quantradin fill options on the far side of the quote, never the mid. I built it for US stocks and options only though, no perps. quantradin.com

replies.author: tommy_johnsen
replies.body: That's really useful, thanks. Filling at the far side of the quote is a good default, and you're right that a trend flip fires just when everyone else's does. I'll start pricing paper fills that way so the results aren't too rosy. Mine's mostly S&P 500 plus perps, so not quite your fit, but the fill lesson carries over.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: perps are where it bites hardest too, with funding on top of a crowded flip. the S&P side is kinder on daily bars as long as you assume the fill comes at the next open, not the close that fired the signal.

replies.author: tommy_johnsen
replies.body: Good call on the next open. Filling at the close that fired the signal would be a sneaky way to fool myself. I'll fill at the next open and charge funding on the perp side. Appreciate it.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: funding is the one people leave out, so good that it's in. if you hold a flip for weeks it can end up costing more than the fills do.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: I don't have live results of my own, so take this as a testing approach. For the confirmation question, run the same flip rule with 0, 1, 2 and 3 candles of confirmation on identical data and costs, and compare average net R per trade, trade count and drawdown. A longer confirmation usually cuts false flips but gives up part of the move, so the answer depends on how much of your edge sits in the first leg. What people commonly report breaking first after paper is fills and slippage on volatile candles, funding costs on held positions, API errors or partial fills that leave state out of sync, and manual overrides. Daily flips also cluster around scheduled macro days, and Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for macro releases) is one source for checking that.
